_metadata.scope: Ancestor levels above the item for all of Book I (Prologue and Distinctions 1–48), Book II Distinction 44, and Book III Distinctions 23–25, together with a complete Book I entry and partial Book II, Book III, and whole-work entries built from them.

ta-l1prol.summary: The Prologue to Book I has a single quaestio. In it Aquinas comments on Lombard's prologue and then sets out a methodological account of sacred doctrine in five articles. Theology is necessary beyond philosophy because the human end is the immediate vision of God, which no creaturely knowledge reaches. It is one science, unified by the divine light under which it considers all things, and it commands the other sciences and uses them as servants. It is principally speculative, a true science whose principles are the articles of faith, and it is wisdom in the highest sense. Its subject is God, together with all things as they come from God and are ordered to God. Its many modes, and the fourfold sense of Scripture, follow from its revealed matter and its ends, with argument reserved to the literal sense. The Prologue thus sets the epistemic terms for the whole Scriptum: a single, contemplative science that rests on revealed principles and is ordered to beatitude.
claims: Sacred doctrine is necessary beyond philosophy because the human end, the vision of God, exceeds what natural reason can attain.
Sacred doctrine is a single, principally speculative science and wisdom, whose principles are the articles of faith and which commands the philosophical disciplines.
Its subject is God and all things as related to God, and its modes of procedure and the senses of Scripture derive from its revealed principles and its ends.

ta-l1d1.summary: Distinction 1 of Book I opens Thomas's commentary on the body of the Sentences with Lombard's Augustinian division of theology's subject matter into things and signs, and of things into what is to be enjoyed (frui) and what is to be used (uti). Four quaestiones work through this division. Quaestio 1 asks what enjoyment and use are. Enjoyment is an act of the will under charity that completes, in delight, the intellect's vision of the divine essence, which is the substance of beatitude. Use is an act of the will executing what reason has ordered to an end. Quaestio 2 treats the objects of enjoyment. God alone is enjoyed as object, while created beatitude and charity are 'enjoyed' only as form or habit, and creatures only 'in God' through the likeness of grace. The three persons are enjoyed by a single enjoyment, because the divine goodness, the formal object, is one. Quaestio 3 holds that everything other than God is to be used, that is, loved in ordering to the first goodness that all things participate. Habitual reference to God suffices, no deliberate act is morally indifferent, and venial sin is excess within a habitual ordering to God. Quaestio 4 limits proper enjoyment to rational knowers who possess the true end: the blessed perfectly, the just imperfectly, and God himself. It holds that use persists in heaven for means that imply no imperfection. Its expositio justifies Lombard's divisions and Augustine's definitions as distinctions by concept and cause. The distinction as a whole sets out the soul's ordering to God as final end: intellect supplies vision and order, will enjoys the end and uses the means, and every created good is loved for God's sake.
claims: Enjoyment is an act of the will under charity that completes the intellect's vision of God; use is the will's execution of what reason orders to the end.
God alone is the object of enjoyment, and the three persons are enjoyed by one enjoyment because the divine goodness is one.
Every created good is to be used, that is, loved in ordering to God; habitual reference suffices, and no deliberate act is indifferent.
Only the blessed enjoy perfectly; the just enjoy imperfectly, and use remains in heaven for means implying no imperfection.

ta-l1d2.summary: Distinction 2 of Book I, a single quaestio, lays the metaphysical foundations of Thomas's Trinitarian theology. Its prooemium sets the whole Sentences within an exitus–reditus scheme, in which things go forth from God as principle and return to him as end. It places Book I as the study of the procession of persons in unity of essence, which is the cause of the procession of creatures. Thomas proves God's unicity from the identity of the divine essence with its esse, which cannot be multiplied, and from the reduction of all multitude to one principle. He then develops his theory of the divine attributes. All creaturely perfections pre-exist in God eminently, really one and conceptually distinct, and their conceptual plurality has a proximate foundation in God's full perfection, which exceeds every created concept. Only the uncreated Word represents God perfectly. On this basis he reconciles the negative and causal theology of Avicenna and Maimonides with the eminence theology of Dionysius and Anselm. He holds on faith, not demonstration, that the one essence, being its own esse, can be numerically one in several supposits. He then holds that the persons are really distinct through relative opposition, while each relation is only conceptually distinct from the essence. The expositio glosses Lombard's text on the right way to investigate the Trinity and its scriptural proofs.
claims: God is one, because his essence is identical with his esse and cannot be multiplied.
The divine attributes are really one and conceptually many, with a proximate foundation in God's perfection, which exceeds every created concept.
The divine essence, being its esse, can be numerically one in several persons, as faith teaches.
The persons are really distinct by opposed relations, each of which is only conceptually distinct from the essence.

ta-l1d3.summary: Distinction 3 of Book I treats what can be known of God through creatures, in five quaestiones that move from natural knowledge to the vestige and image of the Trinity. Quaestio 1 arranges Lombard's proofs of divine unity under the three Dionysian ways of causality, remotion, and eminence. It holds that God is knowable but never comprehensible, and that his existence is self-evident in itself but not to us, so it must be demonstrated from effects; Anselm's argument holds only on a supposition. Knowing God through creatures, grounded in analogical exemplarity, belongs to wayfaring humans, good and bad, while natural reason cannot reach the Trinity, and arguments for it are arguments of fittingness. Quaestio 2 defines the vestige as an imperfect likeness that leads to its source. It locates the vestige in every creature's ordered perfection as beginning, middle, and end, which mirrors the persons, and it treats the traditional triads (number–weight–measure, mode–species–order, and others) as variant assignments of that scheme. Quaestiones 3–5 turn to the image. Only rational creatures bear it, in their contemplative mind, since an image requires determinate representation with consubstantial distinction and equality; the Son alone is the perfect image. The first Augustinian triad, memory, understanding, and will, consists of ordered powers that flow as proper accidents from the soul's essence. They image the Trinity most truly when directed to God, then to the soul itself, and the soul always understands itself and God indeterminately by simple presence. The second triad, mind, knowledge, and love, is a less proper assignment by essence and consubstantial habits. Sin destroys only the image of re-creation, not the image of creation or of likeness. Across the distinction, creation reveals God's essence through analogy and the Trinity only through the imperfect likenesses of vestige and image.
claims: God is knowable but incomprehensible; his existence is not self-evident to us but demonstrable from effects by causality, remotion, and eminence.
Natural reason cannot reach the Trinity; Trinitarian arguments are arguments of fittingness.
Every creature is a vestige of the Trinity through its ordered perfection as beginning, middle, and end.
The image of the Trinity is in the rational mind's powers of memory, understanding, and will, most truly as they bear on God; sin destroys only the image of re-creation.

ta-l1d4.summary: Distinction 4 of Book I begins Lombard's incidental questions about the procession of persons by asking whether essential names can stand as supposit or terminus of generation. It has two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 affirms, on faith, that there is generation in God, understood as the communication of nature in perfect likeness without the change, potency, or division of essence that mark creaturely generation. It states a general rule of divine naming: a name is said properly of God according to its constitutive difference, with the imperfection of its genus removed. On this basis 'God begot God' is simply true, because 'Deus', a concrete name, signifies the essence while of itself suppositing indistinctly for a person. 'God begot another God' and 'God begot himself as God' are false, and propositions with relative clauses are true or false according to appositive or mediate construal. Quaestio 2 holds that true propositions about the simple God are possible. Our intellect, knowing from composite creatures, composes concepts diverse in mode and identical in reality, and it must affirm divine names, deny their creaturely mode, and affirm them super-eminently. Because nature and supposit are indifferent in God, person and essence are predicated of each other convertibly, so 'God is the Father' and 'God is the Trinity' are true while 'one person is three' is false. Throughout, Thomas uses supposition theory and the semantics of abstract and concrete names to keep both the unity of essence and the distinction of persons.
claims: There is generation in God, understood as communication of the same nature without change or composition, and held by faith.
'Deus' signifies the essence but of itself supposits indistinctly for a person, so 'God begot God' and 'God is the Trinity' are true.
True propositions about the simple God compose concepts diverse in mode but identical in reality.
Because nature and supposit are indifferent in God, essence and person are predicated of each other convertibly.

ta-l1d5.summary: Distinction 5 of Book I asks, in three quaestiones, how the divine essence, signified by abstract names, relates to the Son's generation: as begetter, as that from which, and as terminus. Quaestio 1 denies that the essence begets. Acts belong to supposits, with the nature as their principle, and since essence and person differ in God only in mode of signifying, essential acts such as creating may be said of the essence while notional acts such as begetting may not. The Father begets by the power of the nature. Divine names are ranked by their nearness to a distinct supposit, from 'Father' through 'person', 'God', 'nature', and 'substance' to 'essence', the most abstract and least able to bear notional predicates. Quaestio 2 holds that the Son is begotten 'de substantia patris', distinguishing 'de' (consubstantial principle) from 'ex' (mere order of principle). It denies that the Son is from nothing, since he receives numerically the same, non-dependent being as the Father. It notes with Avicenna that even an eternal creature would be from nothing by natural dependence. Quaestio 3 holds that the essence is the terminus of generation as received by the Son, never as generated, and that divine generation has a terminus ad quem but no terminus a quo. It classifies notional verbs: 'give' and 'receive' can take the essence as object, but no notional verb takes it as subject. The expositio glosses Hilary on univocal generation and on the mutual indwelling of Father and Son through the one nature given and retained.
claims: The divine essence neither begets nor is begotten; the Father begets by the power of the nature.
Notional acts are predicated of divine names in proportion to their nearness to a distinct supposit, and least of all of 'essence'.
The Son is begotten from the Father's substance as from a consubstantial principle and is not from nothing.
The essence is the terminus of generation as the nature received by the Son.

ta-l1d6.summary: Distinction 6 of Book I, a single quaestio, asks about the principle of the Son's generation: necessity, will, or nature. Against Eunomius's dilemma, Thomas holds that the generation has the absolute, uncaused necessity of the first cause, not the necessity of coercion or of an end. The Father begot the Son by will only in the sense of concomitant will, willing the generation as its object, as he wills to be God. Will as principle instead grounds the Spirit's procession as love and the free production of creatures, which proceed from antecedent will as things that can be or not be. The Son, who proceeds as Word and art, corresponds to the intellect. The Father begot the Son by nature, since generation, as production in likeness of nature, belongs to the divine essence under the attribute of nature. Nature and will are really one but conceptually distinct principles. The expositio explains the order of will and knowledge and shows that 'nolens' is not the contradictory of 'volens'.
claims: The Son's generation is absolutely necessary, not coerced or for an end.
The Father begot the Son by nature, and by will only concomitantly.
Creation proceeds from God's antecedent, free will; the Spirit proceeds as love, the Son as Word.

ta-l1d7.summary: Distinction 7 of Book I treats the power of begetting in God and whether it is common to Father and Son, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 affirms a power to beget modelled on natural power, by which the Son receives numerically the Father's nature. It contrasts this with the quasi-rational power by which creatures proceed according to divine ideas, to which alone omnipotence refers. Divine power is superactive, acting by operation rather than motion and needing no matter. The power to beget is the divine essence considered as identical with paternity: absolute as rooted in the essence, relative as joined to its act, and so a mean between essential and personal. Personal properties do not contract the common nature. The powers to beget and to create are numerically one in the essence, but as joined to their acts the power to beget is prior, as generation is prior to creation. Quaestio 2 distinguishes impersonal, active, and passive senses of 'potentia generandi'. The power is in the Son as the power by which he is begotten, but not as a power to beget. Neither the Son nor the Father can beget another son, because persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, which cannot be numerically multiplied, and in God being and being able coincide. The impossibility reflects the structure of the persons, not a lack of power, and the Son's not begetting is no impotence, since begetting is opposed to filiation.
claims: There is a power to beget in God, modelled on natural power and not falling under omnipotence, which concerns creatures.
The power to beget is the essence under the aspect of paternity, a mean between absolute and relative.
The power to beget is in the Son only impersonally and passively; there can be only one Father and one Son.
The Son's not begetting is not impotence, because begetting is opposed to filiation.

ta-l1d8.summary: Distinction 8 of Book I begins Lombard's treatment of the divine essence in itself, under the attributes of truth, immutability, and simplicity, in five quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that 'He who is' is God's most proper name, because in him alone being is identical with quiddity. Being belongs to him properly as pure, unmixed with potency, and the way of remotion ends in a darkness of ignorance in which we are best united to God in this life. God is the being of all things causally, not essentially, as an analogical agent. Among the transcendentals, being is first in concept and is the first thing the intellect grasps, while the good is first in causality. Quaestio 2 defends Boethius's definition of eternity as the exclusion of beginning and end, of succession, and of limitation by a receiver. Eternity belongs properly to God alone, and time, aevum, and eternity are distinguished by the relation of potency to act. Tensed predicates are truly said of God according to their perfection. Quaestio 3 holds that God, as pure act, is wholly immutable, and that his eternal operation yields temporal effects by the order of wisdom. Every creature is mutable through potency, and its total dependence on God makes it corruptible only conditionally. Quaestio 4 holds that God is wholly simple, being his own being. He is in no genus, since his being is his quiddity, and only substance and relation remain as modes of predication in him. Quaestio 5 contrasts creaturely simplicity. Every complete creature is composed of quiddity and esse. Universal hylomorphism is rejected, and the soul is composed of essence and esse; its esse is that of the whole human, it is individuated by the body yet survives as an individual, and it is wholly in every part of the body as form. The distinction as a whole develops Thomas's metaphysics of esse: God is subsistent being itself, eternal, immutable, and simple, and creatures receive a finite, composite, mutable being from him.
claims: 'He who is' is God's most proper name, since in God alone being is identical with quiddity.
God is the being of all things causally, as an analogical agent, not essentially.
Eternity belongs properly to God alone; time, aevum, and eternity are distinguished by the relation of potency to act.
God alone is immutable and wholly simple, and is in no genus; every creature is composed of essence and esse and is mutable.
The soul is not hylomorphic but composed of essence and esse; it is individuated by the body, survives as an individual, and is wholly in every part of the body.

ta-l1d9.summary: Distinction 9 of Book I begins Lombard's treatment of the distinct persons with the Son's eternal generation, defended against Arius through Augustine, Ambrose, and Hilary, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 examines the language of the Son's distinction from the Father. The Son is 'alius' but not 'aliud' than the Father: the adjectival masculine bears on the person, while the substantival neuter would imply a diversity of essence. 'Alius' implies diversity of hypostasis, and subsistent divine properties make the persons 'alius'. Essential substantives such as 'God' are never predicated in the plural of the persons, while adjectives can be plural through the plurality of supposits. So 'eternal' is singular or plural according to its construal, and 'coeternal' is always plural. Quaestio 2 denies that the Father is prior to the Son in duration, nature, understanding, or dignity, since the essence is one and relatives are simultaneous, and the Father is constituted by the very paternity that relates him to the Son. It holds that the eternal generation, in which being and perfection coincide, is best signified by 'semper natus'. The expositio explains why God could not newly become Father without change: paternity is a real, constitutive relation in God, unlike his merely conceptual relation to creatures.
claims: The Son's generation is eternal; the Father is in no way prior to the Son.
The Son is alius but not aliud than the Father.
Essential substantives are singular of the persons; adjectives can be plural, and 'coeternal' is always plural.
The eternal generation is best expressed as 'semper natus'.

ta-l1d10.summary: Distinction 10 of Book I, a single quaestio, begins Lombard's treatment of the Holy Spirit's procession by asking about its mode. Thomas argues that as the Son is the exemplar of creatures' natural procession, so the free procession of creatures from God's will must be grounded in a person proceeding as love, the Holy Spirit. Love in God is essential (common to the three and appropriated to the Spirit), personal (proper to the Spirit), or notional (the common spiration of Father and Son). By his mode of procession the Spirit is the mutual love of Father and Son and their bond, uniting them as distinct persons quasi-formally, as a form proceeding from both rather than as their principle. 'Holy Spirit' is his proper name by ecclesial imposition and fittingness. 'Spirit' signifies freedom from matter, through the Spirit as first gift we are drawn into divine spirituality, and 'holy' implies the rectitude proper to will. There are exactly three persons. Persons are constituted by proper relations of origin that pertain to dignity, and the two modes of origin, generation by nature and spiration by will, yield one unoriginate principle, the Father, and two distinct proceeding persons, the Son from one and the Spirit from two. The expositio distinguishes amor, dilectio, and caritas.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds as love, the reason of God's free giving to creatures.
The Spirit is the mutual love and bond of Father and Son.
There are exactly three persons, constituted by relations of origin through generation and spiration.

ta-l1d11.summary: Distinction 11 of Book I, a single quaestio, defends the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son as well as the Father. Thomas argues that without the filioque Son and Spirit could not be distinguished, since divine persons differ only by opposed relations of origin, and different modes of procession from the Father alone would not suffice. Patristic and analogical objections are answered: symbolic theology does not argue, Damascene wrote amid the controversy, and the analogies of word and breath and of the sun's splendour and heat, rightly understood, support the filioque. Father and Son spirate as two agents but one principle, as one in spirative power, which is the essence under the aspect of common spiration, a notion shared by the two. The Spirit does not spirate himself, because the essence in him is not common spiration. Because acts take number from supposits, Father and Son are 'spirators', not 'one spirator', though they are one creator and one principle of the Spirit. The expositio defends the scriptural proofs, reading the genitive 'Spirit of the Son' as a genitive of origin, and justifies the Latin addition to the Creed as an authorized explicitation of what was implicit.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; without this, Son and Spirit could not be distinguished.
Father and Son spirate as one principle, in common spiration, but are plural spirators.
The filioque makes explicit what is implicit in the Creed.

ta-l1d12.summary: Distinction 12 of Book I, a single quaestio, asks whether there is any order between Father and Son in the procession of the Spirit. Thomas holds, with Augustine, that in God there is only an order of nature, by which one is from another without being prior, so the Son's generation precedes the Spirit's procession only in our mode of understanding. The Spirit proceeds neither earlier nor more fully from the Father than from the Son, since Father and Son are one principle with numerically the same spirative power. The Father is called 'principal' and 'proper' principle by his authority of origin, not by any degree, and he is principle, not cause, of the other persons, since cause implies diversity of essence. The procession is both immediate, in the one power and in the Father's supposit, and mediate, through the Son as a spirating person who is from the Father. A general theory of ordered causes holds that the first cause is most immediate in power and the last in agency, so God is most immediate in power to every natural operation, and the Father acts through the Son, never the Son through the Father.
claims: In God there is order of nature without priority; generation does not precede procession.
The Spirit proceeds equally from Father and Son as one principle; the Father's primacy is authority, not degree.
The procession is immediate in power and mediate through the Son as person.

ta-l1d13.summary: Distinction 13 of Book I, a single quaestio, compares the Spirit's procession with the Son's generation. There is procession in God properly, as origination from a principle without change. There are exactly two processions, distinguished not as primitive realities nor by nature and will, which are only conceptually distinct, but by origin: one from one (generation, by way of nature and intellect) and one from two, including the one who proceeds (spiration, by way of will). So again, without the filioque Son and Spirit could not be really distinguished. The processions differ really through the relative properties, which act as their principles and termini, and only conceptually through the nature, and relations as constitutive forms of the persons ground the processions' difference without a vicious circle. 'Procession' and 'generation' relate as common and proper, not as genus and species. The Spirit's procession bears only the common name because creatures offer no subsistent procession by way of love from which to name it, and it is not 'nativity' because it is from the nature as will. 'Unbegotten', as a negation, fits the Spirit in a broad sense, but as a notion it belongs to the Father alone.
claims: There are exactly two processions in God, distinguished by relations of origin.
The Spirit's procession is called by the common name 'procession' because creatures offer no proper analogue.
'Unbegotten' as a notion belongs to the Father alone.

ta-l1d14.summary: Distinction 14 of Book I begins the treatment of the Holy Spirit's temporal procession in three quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that because the Spirit proceeds as love tending into the beloved, the same love by which the Father loves the Son proceeds into creatures as the reason of every gift of love, as the Son is the reason of creation. This temporal procession is a new relation, real only in the creature, and it is essentially one procession with the eternal, twofold only by relation to eternal and created objects, with created grace as the likeness and sign of uncreated love. Quaestio 2 holds that the Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given, since our relation through the gifts terminates in him. It places the Spirit's mission within the exitus–reditus of creation: the processions of the persons ground both creatures' going out from God and their return, and the Spirit is sent strictly only through the gifts that join us immediately to God as end, sanctifying grace and glory. In these gifts the persons seal themselves in the soul and are known quasi-experientially. Quaestio 3 holds that God alone gives the Spirit, because only God can create sanctifying grace, which is not educed from matter, joins us immediately to him, and orders us to the infinite good. Ministers of the Church and sacraments act instrumentally, with efficacy from divine institution.
claims: The Spirit proceeds temporally into creatures as the same love by which the Father loves the Son; eternal and temporal procession are one procession, twofold by relation to its objects.
The Spirit himself is given, but only through sanctifying grace and glory, the gifts of return to God.
God alone gives the Holy Spirit; ministers and sacraments act instrumentally.

ta-l1d15.summary: Distinction 15 of Book I treats divine mission in five quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that mission belongs to the divine persons, purified of local motion and inferiority, as a going out of origin from a principle together with a new mode of the person's presence in the creature. Mission principally signifies the essential ordering to its effect and consequently a notional relation of origin, shared by Son and Spirit. Quaestio 2 holds that only the Son and Spirit, who are from another, can be sent, since mission implies authority of origin, while the whole Trinity comes and indwells. Quaestio 3 holds that the Spirit properly sends himself and that the whole Trinity sends both Son and Spirit, since sending is making the one who is from another be newly in a creature, which requires only efficiency over the effect. The Father sends but cannot be sent. Quaestio 4 holds that as divine goodness proceeds into creatures in their going out, so in their return the persons proceed by received likenesses of their proper relations: the Spirit by love, the Son by wisdom. The Son is sent properly only in a wisdom that breathes forth love, the two missions are distinct but inseparable, and mission is only temporal. Quaestio 5 holds that mission is made to rational creatures capable of grace. It recurs with new uses of grace and, for the blessed, with new revelations, and it was made to Christ's soul once, at his conception. It became fuller after the incarnation through humanity's greater preparation, and it removes us from the world not by place but by conforming knowledge and love to eternal things.
claims: Mission is origin from a principle together with a new presence in the creature; only Son and Spirit are sent, while the whole Trinity sends and indwells.
The Son is sent by the gift of a wisdom from which love proceeds, the Spirit by the gift of love; the two missions are inseparable.
Mission is made only to rational creatures capable of grace and became fuller after the incarnation.

ta-l1d16.summary: Distinction 16 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the visible mission of the Holy Spirit. Visible mission is invisible mission manifested by a visible sign. The Son's visible mission is the incarnation, in which the visible nature is assumed and is itself the terminus. The Spirit's visible forms are only specially instituted signs of present grace, unlike New Law sacraments, which signify and cause grace to come, and visible mission adds to mere apparition the manifestation of origin and indwelling, so the Father can appear but not be sent. Visible mission signifies a fullness of grace overflowing to others, so it was made to Christ and the apostles as founders of the Church. It was not made to the Old Testament fathers, before the time of grace, and it is no longer needed now that the faith is established and its proof complete. The forms signify overflow of grace by operation, sacramental and life-giving (the dove at Christ's baptism, Christ's breath on the apostles), and by teaching (the bright cloud at the transfiguration, the tongues of fire at Pentecost). They are true signs, like metaphors, not true animals or fire. Angels minister the outward signs, but the inner grace is immediately from the divine person. The expositio interprets Hilary's 'the Father is greater' as the dignity of giving, without the Son being lesser.
claims: Visible mission is the manifestation of invisible mission through a sign of overflowing grace.
Visible missions were made to Christ and the apostles to signify grace overflowing by operation and teaching for the planting of the Church.
Angels form the outward signs, but grace is from the divine person immediately.
concepts: dove, cloud, breath, tongues of fire

ta-l1d17.summary: Distinction 17 of Book I treats the Spirit's invisible mission through charity and contains Thomas's sustained disagreement with Lombard's thesis that the charity by which we love is the Holy Spirit himself. Quaestio 1 holds that charity is a created habit and accident in the soul. The soul's goodness in the being of grace requires an inhering form, and perfect, meritorious acts require a perfecting habit, since operations follow the conditions of their proximate causes. Created charity is efficiently from the whole Trinity and exemplarily from the uncreated love that is the Spirit. It is given according to natural capacity together with the disposition of effort, no one can know with certainty that they have it, and it can be loved from charity, since immaterial powers reflect on their own acts. Quaestio 2 holds that charity increases essentially, by intensification rather than addition, as the infused act is brought from imperfect to perfect through the recipient's preparation. An act from one's whole power merits immediate increase, there is no limit in principle to charity's growth, since the soul's capacity grows with what it receives, and charity does not decrease essentially: venial sin affects only its fervour and rootedness, and only mortal sin removes it. In both quaestiones the expositio reinterprets Lombard's authorities as causal predication and judges his replies insufficient.
claims: Charity is a created habit in the soul, not the Holy Spirit himself, against Lombard; it flows exemplarily from the Spirit.
Charity increases essentially by intensification through the recipient's preparation and has no limit in principle.
No one can know with certainty that they have charity; venial sin does not diminish charity, mortal sin removes it.

ta-l1d18.summary: Distinction 18 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the name 'gift' as said of the Holy Spirit. 'Gift' is notional when it implies the giver's authority of origin and essential when it implies only free possession, as the essence is 'given' to the Son. It is proper to the Spirit by his eternal procession, since he proceeds as love, the ground of all free giving, and is therefore gift per se and first. 'Donum' differs from 'datum' as timeless from temporal, as implying liberality, and as aptitude from act, so the Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given, and the Son is given but not gift. Everything God gives to creatures, including the Son given to the world, is given through love, God alone giving with pure liberality, though the Spirit himself is given only in charity. By his procession as emanation the Spirit receives deity, while his relation makes him formally gift. An analysis of possessive pronouns with divine names concludes that the Spirit is 'our given' but not 'our gift', and that God is specially God of the just, who possess him as their end.
claims: 'Gift' is the Spirit's proper name, since he proceeds as love, the ground of all free giving.
Everything God gives creatures is given through love; only God gives with pure liberality.
The Spirit is eternally gift and temporally given.

ta-l1d19.summary: Distinction 19 of Book I treats the equality of the divine persons in five quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that equality and likeness exist in God through species of quantity and quality taken by their differentiae, so the persons are equal by numerically one magnitude. Equality fits them better than identity because it signifies unity of essence together with distinction of persons, and it is mutual, though only the receiving person is 'equalized' to the giver. Quaestio 2 holds that eternity, aevum, and time are distinguished by the kind of act they measure, from pure act without potency to successive act mixed with potency, and that God is his eternity, its 'now' differing only conceptually. Quaestio 3 identifies divine magnitude as the completeness of the divine nature's perfection, one of the three senses of divine virtus alongside power and eternity, and holds that the persons are in one another by unity of essence and by relation. Quaestio 4 holds that the persons share the essence neither as parts of an integral whole nor as instances of a universal: the number of persons is distinction without aggregation, and the essence is common but not universal. Quaestio 5 gives Thomas's theory of truth. Truth is the adequation of intellect and thing, founded on being and completed in judgment. All things are true by one divine truth as exemplar and by many created truths formally, through analogy of intention and being, and only divine truth is eternal and immutable, the soul's grasp of truth proving its immortality.
claims: The persons are mutually equal by numerically one magnitude; equality signifies unity of essence with distinction of persons.
Eternity, aevum, and time are distinguished by the kind of act they measure; God is his eternity.
The persons share the essence neither as parts nor as instances of a universal; the essence is common but not universal.
Truth is the adequation of intellect to being; only divine truth is eternal, and created truths are many and mutable.

ta-l1d20.summary: Distinction 20 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the persons' equality in power. The Son is omnipotent though he cannot beget, because a relation posits something only by its being, which in God is the essence, and by its concept is only toward another. So the Father's paternity and active generation give him nothing the Son lacks, and not begetting is no defect of power. The Son is equal to the Father in omnipotence, sharing numerically one essence and power. Power is appropriated to the Father only by likeness to his property as principle without principle, and in God neither giver nor receiver is defective, so the Son receives the Father's whole power. Among the persons there is an 'order of nature', an order of origin preserved by its differentia without the generic priority of order, so there is neither order simply nor any grade. The expositio defends Augustine's arguments from the numerical identity of what the Son receives and distinguishes what is due to the Son by nature, equality, from what is given to creatures by grace.
claims: The Son is omnipotent and equal to the Father in power, though he cannot beget.
Relations posit nothing beyond the essence, so not begetting is no defect of power.
Among the persons there is order of origin without priority or grade.

ta-l1d21.summary: Distinction 21 of Book I treats exclusive words ('solus', 'tantum') in Trinitarian propositions, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 takes the exclusive word on the subject side. Categorematic 'solus', implying solitude, cannot be said of God, while syncategorematic 'solus', excluding others from the subject's form or from the predicate, can, so 'God alone is God', 'God alone creates', and 'God alone is Father' are true. An exclusive word joined to a supposit excludes every other supposit, even a correlative, and since the Son is another person but not another thing, 'the Father alone is God' is false if it excludes another person and true if it excludes another thing. Quaestio 2 takes the exclusive word on the predicate side. 'The Trinity is the only God' is true, since 'Deus' predicates a subsistent nature. 'The Father is the only God' is false when 'solus' excludes other supposits, since 'Deus' then stands for the Father's supposit, but true when it means 'tantum' or excludes another nature.
claims: Categorematic 'solus' cannot be said of God; syncategorematic 'solus' can.
'The Father alone is God' is false excluding another person and true excluding another thing.
'The Trinity is the only God' is true; 'the Father is the only God' is false when excluding other persons.

ta-l1d22.summary: Distinction 22 of Book I, a single quaestio, gives Thomas's general theory of divine names. God is nameable as he is known, imperfectly, and names himself perfectly only in the Word. Distinguishing the thing signified from the mode of signifying, Thomas holds that names of pure perfections are said properly and first of God as to the thing signified, while names whose meaning includes a creaturely mode are said only metaphorically, so negations are absolutely true and affirmations true as to the thing signified. The many divine names are not synonyms, being founded on the persons, on attribute concepts truly grounded in God, and on negations and relations to creatures. The threefold division of names into metaphorical, common-proper, and personal-proper is sufficient and reconciles Damascene, Dionysius, and Lombard.
claims: God is named imperfectly, as known, and names himself perfectly in the Word.
Names of pure perfections are said properly of God as to the thing signified, not as to the mode of signifying.
The many divine names are non-synonymous, founded on truly distinct concepts in God.

ta-l1d23.summary: Distinction 23 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the name 'person'. Following Boethius, Thomas distinguishes essence, subsistence, and substance by the acts of being, subsisting, and standing under, each taken as quo est or quod est. He defines person as an individual substance of intellectual nature under a property of dignity and explains the Latin–Greek correspondences of usia, usiosis, hypostasis, and prosopon. 'Person' is properly said of God, by the concept of completeness in intellectual nature rather than particularity, since names are judged by what they are imposed to signify, not their origin. In God it signifies relation by way of substance: the distinguishing relation, which is the subsistent person having the divine essence. It is predicated plurally because personality is multiplied with distinct subsistents, which in God are the opposed relations, while 'God' stays singular because deity is one.
claims: Essence, subsistence, and substance are distinguished by esse, subsistere, and substare.
'Person' is properly said of God and signifies relation by way of substance.
There are three persons in one nature, numbered by opposed subsistent relations.

ta-l1d24.summary: Distinction 24 of Book I treats names of unity and plurality in God, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that God is supremely one, as wholly undivided, and that there is in God a certain number, of really subsisting relations, midway between number simply and merely conceptual number. Following Aristotle and Averroes against Avicenna, it distinguishes the transcendental one, which adds only the negation of division, from numerical unity, which adds measure. Only the transcendental one and many apply to God, adding negation conceptually while the persons remain really distinct, and such terms signify essence or notion according to the term they modify. Quaestio 2 gives the rule for Trinitarian language: affirm what opposes both Arius and Sabellius and deny what agrees with either. So the Church affirms unity, simplicity, likeness, and equality of essence, and plurality, distinction, order, and harmony of persons, denying diversity, division, alienness, singularity, uniqueness, confusion, and solitude. 'Trinity' signifies three persons of one essence and is only quasi-collective.
claims: God is supremely one, and there is a number of subsistent relations in God, not quantitative number.
Transcendental one and many add only negation and apply to God; numerical unity does not.
Trinitarian terms are governed by opposition to Arianism and Sabellianism; 'Trinity' means three persons of one essence.

ta-l1d25.summary: Distinction 25 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats 'person' further. Thomas defends Boethius's definition, 'an individual substance of rational nature', taken broadly. Its parts give the genus, the determinate nature, and the intention of particularity. In God definitional composition is only conceptual and individuation is incommunicability grounded in the distinguishing relation. 'Person' is analogical between God and creatures, prior in God as to the thing signified. It is common in the Trinity by a commonness of concept founded in reality, which is not a universal, since the persons share one being. The three persons are three things, from the plurality of relative forms, but not three beings in the substantive sense, since they have one esse. The Expositio rejects the view that 'person' signifies essence in the plural.
claims: Boethius's definition of person, taken broadly, applies to the divine persons.
'Person' is analogical between God and creatures and common in the Trinity by concept, not as a universal.
The three persons are three things but one being.

ta-l1d26.summary: Distinction 26 of Book I treats hypostasis and the personal properties, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that 'hypostasis' is properly said of God and signifies relation as distinct by way of a subsistent in the divine nature. Hypostasis, divine hypostasis, person, and Father are progressively determinate. Since only relation distinguishes in God and the relations subsist without substrate, abstracting the relations leaves no distinct hypostases, though without them God would be one person. Quaestio 2 holds that relations are really in God, founded on the communication of nature, and are both in the persons and identical with them. Four ways in which relations are merely of reason are distinguished, among them God's relations to creatures. Relation, specifically relation of origin, is the only principle of distinction in God, since only relative opposition is free of imperfection. There are five notions, four properties, four relations, and three personal properties.
claims: 'Hypostasis' in God signifies subsistent relation as distinct; abstracting the relations, no distinct hypostases remain.
Relations are really in God and identical with the persons; relations of origin alone distinguish them.
There are five notions, three of them personal.

ta-l1d27.summary: Distinction 27 of Book I treats the notions in relation to the personal names, especially 'Word', in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that the five notions are only three things, since only relatively opposed relations are really distinct. Unopposed relations of one person, like paternity and common spiration, differ as relations by their terms, and Father, paternity, and generation differ only in mode of signifying. Relation, as constituting the person, conceptually precedes the personal operation, though as relation simply it follows it. Quaestio 2 holds that God is properly a Word, as the word of the heart, an emanation from the intellect ordered to manifestation. 'Word' signifies something absolute with a relation of origin, so it can be essential, with a relation of reason, or personal, with a real relation. Usage makes it personal, and so taken it belongs to the Son alone, who proceeds by intellect from one. 'Word' implies relation to creatures only as exemplar or as manifestation to another.
claims: The five notions are three things, distinguished by relative opposition.
Constitutive relation conceptually precedes personal operation.
God is properly a Word; 'Word' can be essential or personal, and personally it is the Son alone.

ta-l1d28.summary: Distinction 28 of Book I treats innascibility and image, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that innascibility is a notion of the Father, who as principle not from a principle is known by innascibility, paternity, and common spiration. 'Unbegotten' is a negation, a quasi-privation without imperfection, founded on the character of principle and reduced to the genus of relation. It is not a personal property, since it presupposes paternity, which alone constitutes the Father and is the formal principle of generation. Quaestio 2 defines image as imitation in an express sign of nature, with equality and an order to an exemplar. Of its three grades the Son is the most perfect image, sharing numerically the same nature. Properly 'image' is personal in God, the essence being exemplar, and it belongs only to the Son, by his procession as Son and Word, not to the Spirit, who proceeds as love.
claims: Innascibility is a notion of the Father, founded on his being principle, but not a personal property.
Image is imitation with equality and order to an exemplar; the Son is the perfect image.
Properly 'image' is personal and belongs to the Son alone.

ta-l1d29.summary: Distinction 29 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats 'principle' in God. One person is principle of another but not cause, since they share one essence and being, and only the Father is author. 'Principle' is analogical between persons and creatures and is said first of the persons absolutely, since their procession exemplifies that of creatures. Common spiration is numerically one notion in Father and Son, since nothing of a special character is numerically multiplied in God. Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by unity of notion, or of spirative power. They are one Creator but not one spirator, since names from personal acts pluralize by supposits while creation is the essence's work. The Expositio explains how the Father is principle of the whole deity.
claims: The Father is principle, not cause, of the Son.
'Principle' is analogical, said first of the persons.
Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by one notion of common spiration.

ta-l1d30.summary: Distinction 30 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats names said of God from time. Relations to creatures are said of God from time, since a relation in act needs both extremes, without any change in God, because relation posits nothing in its subject. Names relating God to creatures as principle signify the essence and belong to the whole Trinity. Names relating God as term, by operation, exemplarity, or the Incarnation, can be personal while including the Trinity as principle. God's relations to creatures are relations of reason founded on his real power and operation: mixed relations in which only the creature's side is real, unlike the mutually real relations of Father and Son.
claims: Temporal names imply no change in God.
They signify the essence as principle and can be personal as term.
God's relations to creatures are of reason, with real foundation.

ta-l1d31.summary: Distinction 31 of Book I treats equality and appropriation in three quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that equality in God is a relation of reason founded on the unity of essence, privative as to its foundation, so a real relation of equality would require the essence to be related to itself. It also holds that essential attributes are appropriated to the persons by the likeness of their concepts to the persons' propers: power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness to the Spirit. Such appropriation is fitting in reality and useful as an imperfect manifestation of the Trinity, without excluding any person. Quaestio 2 explains Hilary's appropriation of eternity to the Father, as principle of duration without principle, beauty to the Son, as the consonance, magnitude, and clarity of the perfect Image, Son, and Word, and use to the Spirit, as Love overflowing as Gift. Quaestio 3 explains Augustine's appropriation of unity to the Father, equality to the Son, and connection to the Spirit, and how all are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, and connected because of the Spirit, both by the order of number and by the persons' properties.
claims: Equality in God is a relation of reason founded on unity of essence.
Attributes are appropriated to persons by likeness to their propers, without excluding the other persons.
Hilary's and Augustine's triads of appropriation rest on likeness to the persons' propers.

ta-l1d32.summary: Distinction 32 of Book I treats locutions comparing the persons by their propers and appropriations, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds, with Hugh of St Victor, that the Father loves the Son by the Holy Spirit, the ablative signifying a quasi-formal effect, since in the genus of action something is denominated by what proceeds from it; so the Father loves and speaks by the persons proceeding as operations, though he does not spirate by the Spirit or beget by the Son. Notionally the Father loves himself by the Spirit too, and Father and Son love us by the Spirit, whose procession is the reason of creatures' free going out and of every gift. Quaestio 2 holds that the Father is not wise by begotten wisdom, since wisdom denominates as an inhering form, which would make the Son a principle of the Father. The Son is wise from the Father efficiently and by essential wisdom formally, and per se through his own hypostasis.
claims: The Father loves the Son, himself, and us by the Spirit, as by a proceeding operation that denominates him.
The Father is not wise by begotten wisdom; the Son is wise from the Father efficiently and by essential wisdom formally.

ta-l1d33.summary: Distinction 33 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the relation of the properties to essence and persons. Against the Porretan doctrine of assisting relations, Thomas holds that the properties are really the divine essence and differ only in concept, since by divine simplicity their being is the essence's being, though relation alone keeps its generic character opposed to substance. Properties and persons are really the same and differ as abstract and concrete, against Praepositinus, who denied properties. Properties are in the essence by identity and in the persons as in supposits, personal properties as constituting and non-personal ones as consequent. Absolute and negative adjectives are said of essence, person, and property alike, but act-adjectives and concrete adjectives belong properly to persons, so 'paternity begets' is improper. Contrary opinions about the notions become heretical only with pertinacity after their consequences for faith are shown.
claims: The properties are really the essence and the persons, distinct only in concept.
Acts and concrete predicates belong properly to persons, not properties.
Error about the notions becomes heresy only with pertinacity.

ta-l1d34.summary: Distinction 34 of Book I, which closes the treatise on the Trinity, has three quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that person and essence are really identical, since the divine nature subsists by itself without individuating matter. They are conceptually distinct, person signifying God as subsistent and proper and essence as simple and common. The three persons are of one essence, the genitive expressing formal causality grounded in the mode of signifying, and are in, not from, one essence. Quaestio 2 defends the appropriation of power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Spirit, both by contrast with creaturely defects of fathers, sons, and 'spirit' and by likeness to the divine propers. Quaestio 3 holds that signifying God by bodily metaphors is most fitting, since we rise from sensibles, sense too is led to God, bodily images show his transcendence by negation, and truth must be hidden from the unworthy, with metaphor resting on likeness of proportionality. Base creatures signify God even more fittingly than noble ones.
claims: Person and essence are really identical; the three persons are of one essence by a genitive of formal cause.
Appropriations work by contrast with creatures and by likeness to the persons' propers.
Metaphor is fitting in theology and rests on proportionality; base images signify God best.

ta-l1d35.summary: Distinction 35 of Book I, a single quaestio, opens the treatment of God as voluntary principle through knowledge, power, and will (Distinctions 35–48) and treats God's knowledge. God is knowing by Dionysius's three ways: removal, since immaterial subsistent form is intelligent; causality, since the first agent directs nature to ends; and eminence. In him knower, known, and knowledge are one, and such names are said properly as to the thing signified. He knows other things through his essence, their likeness, and, against Averroes, knows each thing's proper nature, since he causes all that is in things and orders each to its end. Knowledge is said of God and creatures neither univocally nor purely equivocally but analogically, by imitation. God's knowledge is neither universal, particular, potential, nor habitual, but only actual. The Expositio orders the names of divine knowledge (foreknowledge, disposition, providence, predestination) by conditions on the side of their objects.
claims: God knows himself and all things through his essence, properly and with certainty.
Knowledge is analogical between God and creatures, by imitation.
God's knowledge is pure act.

ta-l1d36.summary: Distinction 36 of Book I treats what God knows and the ideas, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds, against Averroes, Avicenna, and Maimonides, that God knows singulars as singular. As creator of matter and immediate agent in all things, his essence is the likeness of the whole thing, unlike a builder's art. He knows evils through the goods they deprive. Being in God's knowledge, in God, and in his essence are distinguished: creatures are in God as subject to his work and have truer being there, while evils are only in his knowledge. Quaestio 2 holds that ideas exist as the forms of things in God's mind, principles of practical and speculative knowledge, and that Aristotle rejected only separate Forms. There are many ideas, the one essence understood as imitable in many ways, eternally in God's intellect and causing the diversity of things. There are ideas of all things he produces, perfect for composites and imperfect for matter, singulars, and accidents, but none for privation.
claims: God knows singulars and evils through his essence, as cause of matter and form.
Ideas are the divine essence understood as variously imitable; there are ideas of all things God produces.

ta-l1d37.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats the presence and location of spiritual beings in four quaestiones, moving from God to the angels. Quaestio 1 shows that God is essentially and immediately in every creature as the continuous cause of its esse. It then distinguishes a common mode of presence (by essence, presence, and power), a special mode by grace in the saints, and a unique mode by union in Christ. These modes are really grounded in the creature's cumulative conjunction to God and are only rationally distinct on God's side. Quaestio 2 argues that God is properly everywhere, in the spiritual sense of containing and conserving rather than being contained. Such per se omnipresence belongs to God alone because it presupposes infinite power, and it holds only from time, not from eternity, since it is a relation founded on God's operation toward creatures. Quaestio 3 turns to the angel. An angel is in place only through its operation, is in exactly one place at a time because its finite power sustains one operation terminating in one object, and cannot share its proper place with another angel of the same kind of operation. Quaestio 4 treats angelic motion. It is equivocal with respect to bodily motion and non-continuous in its illuminative, intellectual, and local modes. Whether an angel passes through a medium depends on whether it operates there, and its motion is measured by a discrete time of successive 'nows', incommensurable with the continuous time of bodies. One contrast runs through the distinction. God's infinite power and self-identical operation make him present to all things at once and from within, as the giver of esse. The angel's finite operation alone defines its place, its motion, and its time.
claims: God is present in all things essentially, immediately, and properly everywhere as the cause of their esse, with modes of presence (common, grace, union) really grounded in the creature and only rationally distinct in God.
Divine omnipresence belongs to God alone because it presupposes infinite power, and it holds only temporally because it is a relation founded on operation toward creatures.

An angel's place, motion, and time are all constituted by its finite operation: it is in one place at a time, cannot share a proper place with a like angel, moves non-continuously, and is measured by discrete time.
The contrast between divine infinity and angelic finitude of power and operation explains the difference between God's omnipresence and the angel's definitive, single location.

ta-l1d38.summary: Distinction 38 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats God's knowledge in relation to things known. God's knowledge causes goods as an artisan's art joined with will, not evils. It is uniform in its act while knowing the diverse modes of things. God knows enuntiables simply, through his being, the exemplar of all being. He knows actuals by knowledge of vision and possibles by knowledge of simple understanding. He knows future contingents with certainty: effects follow their proximate causes in contingency, and his eternal knowledge, present to all times at once (Boethius), sees each contingent as present in its determinate being. So contingents are necessary relative to his knowledge only conditionally, as what is, when it is, is necessary.
claims: God's knowledge causes goods with will and knows enuntiables and possibles.
God knows future contingents certainly because eternity is present to all times; contingency is preserved by proximate causes and conditional necessity.

ta-l1d39.summary: Distinction 39 of Book I treats the immutability of God's knowledge and his providence, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that God's operative knowledge, commanded by his eternal will, is free: in the divided sense he can not know what he knows and can know what he does not, though not in the composite sense, and his knowledge cannot increase. By simple understanding he knows infinitely many possibles in one non-discursive glance. Quaestio 2 defines providence by addition to knowledge and disposition, as provision of means and removal of obstacles, distinguishing it from governance and from fate, which is providence realized in secondary causes. Against Democritus, Averroes, Maimonides, and the Manichaeans, providence extends to all singulars according to their natures, ordering natural and voluntary evils to good without intending them. The prevalence of human evil is explained by original sin and by human nature's need for acquired or infused virtues.
claims: God's knowledge is immutable yet free in the divided sense; he knows infinitely many possibles.
Providence orders all things to their ends according to their natures, ordering evils to good without intending them.

ta-l1d40.summary: Distinction 40 of Book I treats predestination and reprobation in four quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that predestination is an immanent operation in God, positing nothing in the predestined but its temporal effect, grace and glory. It is a special providence over rational creatures, directed to supernatural ends, with purpose of will and foreknowledge of the outcome, distinct from the book of life. Quaestio 2 holds that predestination is of grace and glory and of those who will attain glory through grace, including future persons known by vision, angels, and Christ as man. Quaestio 3 holds that the number of the predestined is certain to God, formally and materially, without imposing necessity, since effects follow proximate causes and God's eternal knowledge regards things as present. Quaestio 4 holds that reprobation foreknows fault without causing it and wills and causes the punishment that orders it, and that hardening has its first cause in the person's refusal of grace, God only permitting and ordering it.
claims: Predestination is a special providence in God whose effect is grace and glory.
The number of the predestined is certain to God without imposing necessity.
Reprobation causes punishment, not fault; God permits and orders hardening.

ta-l1d41.summary: Distinction 41 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the causes of predestination and the immutability of God's knowledge. Election is eternal in purpose and temporal in execution, and it conceptually precedes predestination as disposition precedes providence. Foreknowledge of merits does not cause predestination, whose only cause is God's goodness, though God wills that grace-informed merits cause glory and that preparation dispose to grace. So glory follows distributive justice and grace liberality. Predestination's effect is helped by condign and congruous merit, prayer, disposition, and natural causes, which it includes as means. God knows every thing he once knew, though tensed enuntiables change in truth.
claims: Predestination has no cause in our merits but includes merits and prayers as causes of its effects.
Election precedes predestination.
God's knowledge is immutable though tensed propositions change.

ta-l1d42.summary: Distinction 42 of Book I begins the treatment of God's power, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that power belongs to God most perfectly, as pure act who acts on all and is acted on by nothing. His power is his essence as principle of operation, needing no matter, and it is one, really many only in its effects. Quaestio 2 holds that God causes creaturely acts as first cause but cannot do what belongs to limited natures, nor sin. He can do whatever does not imply contradiction, including what is impossible to nature, but not the per se impossible, like undoing the past. Miracles are above or beside nature, not against it, since matter has obediential potency. Relative possibility is judged by proximate causes, and effects immediate from God are judged by God.
claims: God's power is his essence, one and perfect.
God can do all that does not imply contradiction; he cannot sin or undo the past.
Miracles are above or beside nature.

ta-l1d43.summary: Distinction 43 of Book I treats the infinity of God's power and the freedom of his action, in two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that God's essence is infinite negatively, his being unreceived and so unlimited, and that his power is infinite as following from it. Omnipotence cannot be communicated to any creature, since power follows essence and every created essence is finite, received being. Quaestio 2 holds that God does not act by necessity of nature but by the order of his wisdom and his free will, as shown in the arrangement of the heavens. He can do nothing unjust, yet justice does not determine him to one course, since his will is the source of created justice, and his mercy is consistent with the justice of his goodness.
claims: God's power is infinite because his being is unreceived; omnipotence is incommunicable.
God creates freely, not by natural necessity, and his justice does not bind him to one course.

ta-l1d44.summary: Distinction 44 of Book I, a single quaestio, asks whether God could make things better. He could improve things accidentally and make better things, but not improve a thing essentially while it remains itself, since that would change its species, like adding a unit to a number. He could make a better universe, by adding species or improving all its parts, though this one is best given its parts, its perfection lying in the diversity of natures filling the grades of goodness. Christ's humanity, the Mother of God, grace, and the ordered universe have a relative infinite dignity from their relation to God. Christ as man cannot be bettered, and Mary's purity, free of original and actual sin, is unsurpassable among creatures. God's power never diminishes, though past and present things cease to be possible objects.
claims: God could make better things and a better universe, but not improve a thing essentially while it remains itself.
Christ's humanity cannot be bettered; Mary's purity is unsurpassable among creatures.
God's power never diminishes.

ta-l1d45.summary: Distinction 45 of Book I, a single quaestio, begins the treatment of God's will. God has will and delight, since will follows intellect, with love but not appetite. He wills his goodness first and creatures as sharing it, out of liberality. His will completes the causality of his indeterminate power and specifying knowledge and is the first cause of things, without excluding secondary causes, which share the dignity of causing. His will of good pleasure, said properly, is distinguished from five metaphorical signs of will: precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation, which correspond to providence over human goods and evils.
claims: God has will, wills creatures out of liberality, and his will is the first cause of things.
God's will of good pleasure is distinguished from five signs of will.

ta-l1d46.summary: Distinction 46 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats God's will and evil. By antecedent will, considering human nature, God wills all to be saved; by consequent will, considering all circumstances, he wills the salvation of those who consent, the distinction lying in the conditions of the thing willed. It is not good that evils happen, though it is good that they are occasions of good. Evil contributes to the universe's perfection only per accidens, through defectible natures and goods occasioned by it, and sin leaves the world worse. God does not will evils to happen but wills to permit them, by willing defectible natures, and to order them.
claims: God wills all to be saved antecedently, the consenting consequently.
God permits and orders evils without willing them; evil perfects the universe only per accidens.

ta-l1d47.summary: Distinction 47 of Book I, a single quaestio, treats the efficacy of God's will. Consequent will is always fulfilled, antecedent will not necessarily. Things happen beside but not against consequent will, and nothing beyond his permission, which regards the cause's power to either opposite. Evils serve God's will passively by falling into the order of punishment, so the wicked do not merit by serving. God can command acts disordered toward creatures by ordering them to himself, as with Abraham's sacrifice, so he dispenses from the second table of the Decalogue but never from the first, which orders immediately to him.
claims: God's consequent will is always fulfilled, and even evils serve it.
God can dispense from precepts of the second table, never the first.

ta-l1d48.summary: Distinction 48 of Book I, a single quaestio, closes the book by treating the conformity of human to divine will. Our will can be conformed to God's by imitation, in its act, where merit lies. Conformity consists essentially in willing good as God ordered and for his glory, perfected by charity, not in agreement about the thing willed. All are bound to it, directly to right willing and indirectly to charity. The deliberate will must conform to God's known will, though natural will and sensitive appetite may rightly shrink, as Christ's and Mary's did at the passion; wayfarers need only not resist, while the blessed rejoice. The Expositio justifies proceeding from God to creatures because faith rests on first truth, anticipating knowledge in the Word.
claims: Conformity to God's will consists in willing good as he ordered, perfected by charity.
All are bound to it; the deliberate will must accept God's known will, though lower appetites may shrink.

ta-l2d44.summary: Distinction 44, the last of Book II, moves from the act of sin to the power to sin, and from there to authority (praelatio) and the obedience owed to it. It has two quaestiones. Quaestio 1 holds that the power to sin, insofar as it is a power, is from God. The defect that lets it fail, which is rooted in the creature's coming from nothing, is in no way from God. The same principle-and-defect structure is applied to prelacy, analyzed by its principle (mode of acquisition), its form (the order of ruler to ruled), and its use. Every prelacy is from God simply by its form, while an unjust principle or use is not from God, except in the qualified sense that God may permit it as just punishment of subjects. Quaestio 1 also distinguishes governing prelacy, ordered to the subjects' good, from dominative prelacy, ordered to the ruler's own good. Dominion over irrational creatures, and directive governance among humans, would have existed without sin. Domination of one human by another presupposes sin. Quaestio 2 treats obedience. It is a special virtue and a part of justice, and it is called 'mother of the virtues' because it disposes to the other virtues. The debt of obedience to secular rulers follows the divine origin of prelacy's form. Personal unworthiness does not void it, but violent or simoniacal acquisition does, and commands that contradict prelacy's purpose may be refused. Baptism does not dissolve servitude, since it removes guilt without at once removing temporal penalties. Religious are bound only to the obedience their rule specifies, and unbounded obedience is praiseworthy but not required. The Expositio textus places the power to sin within the power of prelacy and settles conflicts between authorities by asking whether the lower power derives from the higher wholly or only in part. Throughout, what is positive in a power or an authority is from God, defect is not, and the debt of obedience is measured by each authority's proper ordination.
claims: In both the power to sin and prelacy, what is positively power or form is from God, while defect (rooted in creation ex nihilo, or in an unjust principle or use) is not from God except in a qualified sense.
Prelacy divides into a governing mode compatible with unfallen rational nature in its directive use and a dominative mode over humans that is a consequence of sin.

Obedience is a special virtue, a part of justice, and the debt of obedience, whether to secular or religious superiors, is measured by the proper ordination of the authority, not extended to its logical maximum.
concepts: ex nihilo as root of defectibility

ta-l3d23.summary: Distinction 23 opens the Book III treatise on the virtues. It treats them first in general and then faith in itself and in its formation. Question 1 sets out the framework. Rational powers are not determined to the good by nature, so they need habits that make the rule's rectitude their own second nature. Habits are known through their acts and by reflection, though no one can be certain of having charity. Virtue is a habit, distinct from power, passion and act. Virtues are intellectual, moral or theological, and the theological virtues are needed because humanity's end, the enjoyment of God, exceeds nature. There are exactly three, faith, hope and charity, matching knowledge of the end, confidence in reaching it, and love of it. Question 2 treats faith itself. It defends Hebrews 11:1 as defining faith by its object (first truth, unseen) and its end (the good hoped for). Belief is assent caused by the will's command on account of God's testimony, so it exceeds science in firmness though not in evidence. Faith resides in the speculative intellect, it is a theological rather than an intellectual virtue, it is one because its object is simple, and it is naturally prior to the other virtues. Question 3 explains how charity forms faith: the perfected will gives faith a common form and end while faith keeps its own species. Unformed faith is an infused gift but not a virtue. Demons have only a compelled faith and heretics lose infused faith entirely. When charity comes, the same faith becomes formed. Together the questions set out the psychology of habit and the nature of faith on which the rest of the treatise depends.
claims: Human rational powers need habits, because only an inherent, quasi-natural rectitude determines them to the good, and virtue is such a habit.
The theological virtues are required because humanity's end exceeds nature, and they are exactly three: faith, hope and charity.
Faith is the intellect's assent to first truth, commanded by the will on account of divine testimony, firmer than science though lacking evidence.
Faith is a theological virtue resident in the intellect, one in its object, and naturally prior to the other virtues.
Charity forms faith as the common form and end given by the perfected will, and the same faith passes from unformed to formed.

ta-l3d24.summary: Distinction 24, in a single question, treats faith in relation to its object and to human knowledge. First truth is the formal object of faith, through which anything is credible, as light makes colour visible. Created realities such as the passion are its material object. The object is propositional, and the articles' tensed variation is merely accidental, so the faith of the patriarchs and of Christians is essentially the same. Nothing false can fall under faith, since it rests on infallible first truth and regards contingents as divinely foreknown. Faith is neither vision nor science of its per se objects, since neither God nor the articles are evident in this life. Preambles such as God's existence can be demonstrated and are believed only per accidens. Human reason defends the faith but does not prove it, and miracles attest the messenger, not the message. The objects of faith are known imperfectly, through words and likenesses, 'in a mirror and an enigma'. Faith is necessary because humanity is ordered to a supernatural end and because natural knowledge of God is difficult, rare and late. Believing the unseen on divine authority is praiseworthy and meritorious, and arguments for or against faith of themselves increase its merit. The distinction defines faith as a certain but non-evident cognition of first truth, between ignorance and vision.
claims: First truth is the formal object of faith, and what is believed about God, including created realities, is its material object.
Faith concerns propositions whose temporal aspect is accidental, so faith is the same across history.
Faith is neither vision nor science of its proper objects, though the preambles of faith can be demonstrated.
Faith is necessary for the supernatural end, and believing on divine authority is meritorious, with reasoning about faith increasing rather than diminishing its merit.

ta-l3d25.summary: Distinction 25 treats faith in relation to believers, chiefly through the content that must be believed. Question 1 defines the article of faith. Following Richard of St Victor, an article is an indivisible truth about God with its own special difficulty, accepted on God's testimony and binding by necessity of the end. Creeds legitimately gather the faith of Scripture, and later creeds explain or make explicit what the Apostles' Creed contains. The articles number fourteen by content (seven on the divinity, seven on Christ's humanity) and twelve by apostolic authorship. They are distinguished by distinct difficulties, with omnipotence as the root of faith and the sacraments falling under the article on the Church. Question 2 asks how much must be believed explicitly. Every adult needs some explicit faith, since merit depends on faith directing intention, and God supplies it to anyone who does what lies in them. The measure is what suffices to direct one to the end. It is greater for those charged with teaching, and the lesser rest their implicit faith in teachers only insofar as those teachers conform to God, the first rule. Historically, explicit faith grew until it was completed in Christ. Before the fall implicit trust in providence sufficed. Between the fall and Christ the greater believed explicitly and the lesser implicitly in the redeemer's nativity, passion, resurrection and judgment, and gentiles could be saved by implicit faith. After Christ all must believe explicitly in the redeemer and the Trinity. The distinction thus gives a structured and historically graded account of faith's content.
claims: An article of faith is an indivisible, difficult truth about God, believed on divine testimony and necessary for salvation, and the articles number fourteen by content.
Creeds gather and make explicit the faith of Scripture without adding to its essentials.
Some explicit faith is necessary for every adult; its measure depends on what directs intention to the end and on one's teaching office.
Explicit faith developed historically and was completed in Christ, after whom all must believe explicitly in the redeemer and the Trinity.

ta-l1.summary: Book I of the Scriptum, in its Prologue and forty-eight distinctions, treats God in himself: the one divine essence, the Trinity of persons, and God as the knowing, powerful, and willing principle of creatures. The Prologue defines sacred doctrine as a single, principally speculative science whose principles are the articles of faith and whose subject is God and all things as related to God.
