Distinction 1 orders all things to God as end: God alone is enjoyed, and every created good is used, loved for his sake. Distinctions 2–3 set the work within an exitus–reditus scheme and lay the metaphysical groundwork. God is one because his essence is his esse, his attributes are really one and conceptually distinct, and natural reason knows God through creatures by analogy but cannot reach the Trinity, which creatures reflect only as vestige and image. Distinctions 4–7 treat the Son's generation through the semantics of divine names: generation is communication of nature without change, the essence neither begets nor is begotten, and the Father begets by nature. Distinction 8 develops the metaphysics of esse: God is subsistent being, eternal, immutable, simple, and in no genus, while creatures are composed of essence and received esse. Distinctions 9–13 establish the Son's coeternity and the Spirit's procession as love from Father and Son, exactly three persons being constituted by relations of origin. Distinctions 14–18 treat the missions: the persons are sent into creatures only through sanctifying grace, the Spirit as Love and Gift, and, against Lombard, charity is a created habit. Distinctions 19–20 establish the persons' equality in eternity, magnitude, and power and give Thomas's theory of truth. Distinctions 21–22 treat the logic of exclusive terms and a general theory of divine names. Distinctions 23–30 treat the persons' names and properties: 'person' and 'hypostasis' signify subsistent relation; unity and number in God are transcendental; relations are really in God and identical with the persons, relations of origin alone distinguishing them; there are five notions, three of them personal; 'Word' and 'Image' belong personally to the Son; and names said of God from time imply only relations of reason in him. Distinctions 31–34 complete the Trinitarian treatise: equality is a relation of reason; attributes are appropriated to persons by likeness to their propers (Hilary's and Augustine's triads; power, wisdom, goodness); the Father loves the Son by the Spirit as by a proceeding operation; properties, persons, and essence are really one and conceptually distinct, against Gilbert of Poitiers; and metaphor is fitting in theology. Distinctions 35–41 treat God's knowledge. He knows himself and all things, singulars and evils included, through his essence, the exemplar of the many ideas. His knowledge is analogical to ours, causes goods together with his will, and knows future contingents with certainty because eternity is present to all times. It grounds providence, which extends to all things according to their natures, and predestination, a special providence whose effect is grace and glory, uncaused by merits but including them as means. Distinction 37 treats God's presence in all things as cause of esse and the location of angels. Distinctions 42–44 treat God's power: it is his infinite essence, incommunicable, able to do all that implies no contradiction, freely exercised by wisdom and will, and able to make better things and a better universe, though this one is best given its parts. Distinctions 45–48 treat God's will: he wills creatures out of liberality, his will completes his causality, and he wills all to be saved antecedently and the consenting consequently. He permits and orders evils without willing them, his consequent will is always fulfilled, he can dispense from the second table of the Decalogue but not the first, and human wills are bound to conform to his by charity. Across the book, the procession of the persons in one essence is presented as the cause and exemplar of the procession of creatures and of their return to God, and God's knowledge, power, and will as the complete character of his causality.
claims: Book I treats theology as a revealed science of God and all things ordered to God, who is known naturally by analogy but not as Trinity.

The one divine essence, identical with its esse, is shared by exactly three persons, subsistent relations distinguished only by relative opposition, with the Spirit proceeding as love from Father and Son.
The persons are sent into creatures through sanctifying grace, and their processions are the cause and exemplar of creation and return.

God knows all things, including singulars, evils, and future contingents, through his essence; his providence extends to all things, and predestination is uncaused by merits though it includes them as means.
God's power is infinite and free, extending to all that implies no contradiction, and this universe is best given its parts though a better one is possible.
God wills creatures out of liberality, permits and orders evils without willing them, and human wills are bound to conform to his by charity.

ta-l2.summary: This summary of Book II is partial. It rests only on Distinction 44, the book's last division (1 of its 44 direct divisions), and should not be read as an account of Book II as a whole. Distinction 44 closes the book's treatment of sin by asking where the power to sin comes from, and it then extends the analysis to authority and obedience. The power to sin, insofar as it is a power, is from God. Its defectibility, rooted in creation from nothing, is not. Prelacy is likewise from God in its form, though not necessarily in its acquisition or use. Governing prelacy would have existed without sin, while the domination of one human by another is a consequence of sin. Obedience is a special virtue, a part of justice, whose debt is measured by the proper ordination of each authority, secular or religious. The preceding distinctions are not yet interpreted and are not represented here.
claims: On the evidence of Distinction 44, Book II attributes the power to sin, as power, to God while denying that its defect is from God.
On the evidence of Distinction 44, Book II grounds political and religious authority in the divine origin of prelacy's form and measures the debt of obedience by each authority's proper ordination.

ta-l3.summary: This summary of Book III is partial. It rests only on Distinctions 23, 24 and 25 (3 of the book's 40 direct divisions), which together form the opening of the treatise on faith within Book III's account of the virtues. It does not cover the Christology of Distinctions 1–22 or the later treatment of hope, charity, the cardinal virtues, the gifts and the commandments, and should not be read as an account of Book III as a whole. In the interpreted distinctions, Aquinas first gives a general theory of virtue. Rational powers are rectified by habits, virtue is a habit, and the theological virtues are needed because the human end exceeds nature. He then treats faith in itself. Faith is the intellect's assent to first truth, commanded by the will on account of divine testimony, firmer than science but without evidence. It is a theological virtue, one in its object, and formed by charity, with the same habit passing from unformed to formed. Next he treats faith in its object. First truth is formal, created realities material, and the propositional articles are the same in substance across history; faith is neither vision nor science, though its preambles can be demonstrated. Finally he treats faith in believers: the fourteen articles gathered in the creeds, and the graded, historically developing obligation of explicit faith, completed in Christ and differentiated by teaching office. Within this scope the book presents faith as a supernatural, will-moved cognition of first truth that orders human life to an end beyond nature.
claims: On the evidence of Distinctions 23–25, Book III grounds the virtues in a theory of habit and derives the theological virtues from humanity's supernatural end.
On the evidence of Distinctions 23–25, Book III treats faith as assent to first truth commanded by the will, formed by charity, certain without evidence, and distinct from both vision and science.

On the evidence of Distinction 25, Book III holds that the content of explicit faith is articulated in fourteen articles and that its required extent varies with historical state and ecclesial office.

aquinasscriptum.summary: This summary of Aquinas's Scriptum on the Sentences is partial. It rests on a complete summary of Book I and on partial summaries of Books II and III, built from fifty-three divisions: all forty-nine divisions of Book I (the Prologue and Distinctions 1–48), Book II Distinction 44, and Book III Distinctions 23–25. Book IV is not represented at all, and Books II and III are represented only by the distinctions named. Within that scope, the work opens by defining sacred doctrine as a unified, principally contemplative science that rests on revealed principles and is ordered to the vision of God, with God and all things as related to God as its subject, and it sets the whole within an exitus–reditus scheme in which things go forth from God and return to him. Book I, now interpreted in full, lays the foundation of that scheme. God, whose essence is his very esse, is one, simple, eternal, immutable, infinite, first truth, and the analogical cause of all being. He is known by natural reason through creatures but never comprehended, and named imperfectly by non-synonymous names true as to the thing signified. In that one essence three equal persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, the persons being themselves subsistent relations. Their eternal processions are the cause and exemplar of creatures' going out from God, and their temporal missions through sanctifying grace are the means of creatures' return. As principle of creatures, God acts by knowledge, power, and will. He knows all things, singulars, evils, and future contingents included, through his essence and its ideas. His power extends to all that implies no contradiction and is exercised freely by wisdom, not by natural necessity. His will, out of liberality, causes all goods, permits and orders evils without willing them, and governs all things by a providence that preserves their natures and includes predestination to grace and glory. The Book II material traces the power to sin and the authority of prelates to God as to their positive being, and their defect to creaturely finitude. The Book III material makes the epistemic foundation of theology concrete: faith is the intellect's will-commanded assent to first truth, formed by charity, which is itself a created habit, and its articles are the revealed principles on which theology proceeds. A recurring pattern of explanation runs through the interpreted material. What is positive in creatures (being, truth, power, authority, virtue) is traced to God as cause, defect and limitation to the creature's finitude and composition, and the supernatural end requires supernaturally infused habits beyond nature. No claim is made here about the content of the uninterpreted parts of Books II–IV.
claims: Within the interpreted material, the Scriptum frames theology as a single revealed science whose principles are the articles of faith and whose subject is God and all things as related to God, going forth from and returning to him.

Within the interpreted material, God is subsistent, infinite being and first truth, and the processions of three equal persons, subsistent relations in one essence, are the cause and exemplar of creation, while their missions through sanctifying grace bring about creatures' return.

Within the interpreted material, God causes creatures by knowledge, power, and free will, knowing all things through his essence, able to do all that implies no contradiction, and governing all by a providence that permits and orders evil without willing it.

Within the interpreted material, natural reason reaches God's existence and attributes through creatures by analogy but not the Trinity, which rests on faith, the will-commanded assent of the intellect to first truth.

Within the interpreted material, a common explanatory pattern recurs: what is positive is traced to God as cause, defect and limitation to the creature's finitude, and the supernatural end requires infused habits beyond nature.
